content: The document titled Module 2: Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in September 2023. It provides detailed guidance on the surveillance of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS), a severe outcome of rubella infection, and emphasizes the importance of its prevention through vaccination. 1. Introduction to CRS Surveillance: Rubella surveillance often misses cases due to the mild or asymptomatic nature of the disease. CRS, however, represents the most severe consequence of rubella infection, and its prevention is the primary goal of rubella vaccination. CRS surveillance enables the detection of infants with clinical manifestations, standardizes reporting for regional and global comparisons, and facilitates early intervention to control infection and prevent further spread. Infants with CRS can shed the virus for up to a year or longer, making early detection critical. 4. Objectives of CRS Surveillance: The primary objective is to support national goals related to rubella vaccination, including monitoring progress toward disease elimination. Specific objectives include: Monitoring the impact of rubella vaccination on reducing CRS incidence. Rapidly detecting and isolating affected infants. Mitigating the disease's consequences for infants and families through early medical care. Demonstrating the elimination of rubella and CRS. 5. Separate Surveillance for Rubella and CRS: While rubella and CRS are linked, their surveillance systems differ significantly in case definitions, target age groups, and detection sites. Member States in the South-East Asia Region should develop CRS surveillance systems to capture most suspected cases. Countries without existing systems may start with sentinel sites and expand coverage over time. 6. Types of Surveillance: Minimal Surveillance: Case-based surveillance at sentinel sites with laboratory confirmation is recommended. The primary target group is infants under 12 months of age. Due to the specificity required, laboratory confirmation is critical. Enhanced Surveillance: A national case-based system (passive, active, or both) with laboratory confirmation at health facilities is recommended. 7. Case Detection and Definitions: Suspected Case: Health workers should suspect CRS in infants under 12 months with congenital heart disease (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis), hearing impairment, or specific eye signs (e.g., cataracts, congenital glaucoma, or loss of night/side vision). CRS should also be suspected in infants with a maternal history of rubella infection during pregnancy. Case Definition: Symptoms may include lack of response to sounds, clouded eye lenses, excessive tearing, sensitivity to bright light, or slow growth. Infants may also exhibit rapid or labored breathing. 8. Case Reporting: Passive reporting from sentinel sites is the most common method. Secondary and tertiary care facilities, such as children’s hospitals and centers for hearing and blindness, are ideal reporting sites. Obstetric centers and private clinics caring for pregnant women with rubella should also be included. 9. Role of the Nodal Person: A nodal person is essential to coordinate between specialties (e.g., pediatrics, obstetrics, cardiology, ophthalmology). Responsibilities include collecting clinical and epidemiological data, ensuring specimen collection and transport, maintaining a line list of suspected cases, and communicating with the national coordinator. 10. Linkages with Other Surveillance Programs: WHO’s South-East Asia Regional Office established an online integrated database for newborn birth defects (SEAR-NBBD) in 2014. This network supports data management for birth defects and stillbirths and should be used to report suspected CRS cases. 11. Investigation of Suspected Cases: Case Investigation Form: Suspected cases should be investigated within 48 hours of reporting. A form should be completed following clinical evaluation for CRS-related signs and symptoms. Unique ID: Each case should be assigned a unique identification number, including geographic location, year, and serial number. All related communications and forms should reference this ID. 12. Specimen Collection: Biological specimens are essential for laboratory confirmation. Two types of specimens should be collected: one for virus detection/isolation and another for antibody detection. Nasopharyngeal swabs are preferred for virus isolation, while urine samples are also commonly used. Dried blood spots are an alternative in remote locations where serum transport is challenging. 13. Laboratory Testing: Laboratory-confirmed CRS cases meet one of the following criteria: For infants under 6 months: Detection of rubella IgM antibodies. For infants 6–12 months: Detection of rubella IgM and IgG antibodies, or sustained rubella IgG levels on two occasions at least one month apart (without rubella vaccination or exposure to wild-type rubella). Detection of rubella virus by viral culture or PCR in appropriate clinical samples (e.g., throat/nasal swabs, blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid). Serology results cannot confirm CRS after suspected cases have received rubella vaccination.
